meta.title: Who really said "If we are to achieve a richer culture, rich in contrasting values, we must recognize the whole gamut of human potentialities, and so weave a less arbitrary social fabric, one in which each diverse human gift will find a fitting place"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Margaret Mead wrote it. The line closes a paragraph in Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies (1935), p. 322. Still in copyright.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If we are to achieve a richer culture, rich in contrasting values, we must recognize the whole gamut of human potentialities, and so weave a less arbitrary social fabric, one in which each diverse human gift will find a fitting place'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: the line is genuinely Margaret Mead's, from Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies (1935), p. 322 — unlike the famous Mead lines that aren't.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Mead wrote it in Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies (New York: William Morrow, 1935), where Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ and Lib Quotes ↗ both place it at p. 322, closing a paragraph about how Western culture uses sex as its most striking artificial distinction. The wording that circulates online matches the wording in the book — no paraphrase, no drift.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies

source.excerpt: Historically our own culture has relied for the creation of rich and contrasting values upon many artificial distinctions, the most striking of which is sex. It will not be by the mere abolition of these distinctions that society will develop patterns in which individual gifts are given place instead of being forced into an ill-fitting mould. If we are to achieve a richer culture, rich in contrasting values, we must recognize the whole gamut of human potentialities, and so weave a less arbitrary social fabric, one in which each diverse human gift will find a fitting place.
trail: The line is not floating free. Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ files it under Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies (1935) and gives a page: p. 322.
Lib Quotes ↗ reproduces the whole paragraph the sentence closes, with the same citation — the surrounding text is what makes the attribution checkable rather than merely repeated.
Wikipedia’s article on the book ↗ confirms the 1935 publication by William Morrow in New York, and summarises the argument the sentence caps.

The book’s concluding chapter, reprinted in Michael Kimmel’s The Gendered Society Reader ↗, sets out the Arapesh–Mundugumor–Tchambuli comparison the sentence draws on — though that excerpt stops before the passage itself.
source.cutTag: Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies (1935), p. 322
source.excerptNote: The famous sentence is the last of three. Read alone it sounds like a call to abolish difference, which is the opposite of what the paragraph argues. Note also that the 2001 Harper Perennial reissue is repaginated, so the p. 322 citation belongs to the original Morrow printing.
source.rightsHolder: The Estate of Margaret Mead and HarperCollins Publishers (William Morrow / Harper Perennial)
source.rightsNote: Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies was first published in 1935 by William Morrow in New York — comfortably after the pre-1931 line that marks the US public domain in 2026 — and it is still a commercially published book: the Harper Perennial centennial edition of 2001 ↗ remains in print. Treat the text as in copyright and quote it as a short excerpt with attribution.

author.name: Margaret Mead
author.heading: Who was Margaret Mead?
author.metaLine: 1901–1978 · American cultural anthropologist and museum curator
author.bio: Margaret Mead (1901–1978) was the American cultural anthropologist who did more than anyone else to move the discipline out of the seminar room and into public argument, through books like Coming of Age in Samoa (1928) and Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies (1935). She spent much of her career as curator of ethnology at the American Museum of Natural History in New York, and later taught at Columbia, Fordham and the University of Rhode Island. She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom posthumously in 1979 — and, in a fate she might have found instructive, became one of the internet’s most-quoted people largely on the strength of lines she is not documented as having written.

misattribution.heading: Real — but keeping bad company
misattribution.intro: This one checks out, which is worth saying plainly, because Margaret Mead is one of the internet’s most reliable magnets for undocumented quotations. The lines most often stamped with her name are precisely the ones nobody can find in her books — so a Mead quote deserves a page number before it deserves your trust.

items.scope: “Never doubt that a small group of thoughtful, committed citizens can change the world; indeed, it’s the only thing that ever has.”
items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ found no evidence of the saying in Mead’s own works, identified Donald Keys as the crucial early propagator without establishing how he learned it, and would only tentatively assign it to her. Wikiquote lists it as disputed ↗.

items.scope: “The first sign of civilisation is a healed femur.”
items.why: Wikiquote files the anecdote as disputed ↗, noting it sits awkwardly against Mead’s own 1968 account of civilisation in terms of cities, division of labour and record-keeping, and that it surfaces mainly in later self-help and devotional writing.

items.scope: “Always remember that you are absolutely unique. Just like everyone else.”
items.why: Also in Wikiquote’s disputed section ↗: printed as “Meade’s Maxim” in a 1979 book without being tied to her, and only attached to Mead by name around 2001.

items.scope: This quote, reprinted with no source at all
items.why: The wording itself is accurate wherever it appears, but the citation is stripped: QuoteFancy ↗ and PassItOn ↗ both give the line with nothing but Mead’s name — no book, no year, no page. That is exactly how the fabricated Mead quotes are presented too, which is why the check is worth doing.

misattribution.truthLine: The line on this page is the exception that proves the pattern: Wikiquote files it in its sourced section ↗ under Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies (1935) at p. 322, and Lib Quotes reproduces the whole paragraph it closes ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Mead built Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies around a comparison of three peoples of New Guinea. Among the Arapesh she found men and women alike raised to be co-operative, unaggressive and responsive to others; among the Mundugumor, both sexes raised to be ruthless and aggressive; among the Tchambuli, a division of temperament by sex that ran opposite to the Western expectation. If traits her readers called feminine could be the masculine pattern in one place and outlawed for both sexes in another, she argued, there was no longer any basis for treating them as sex-linked at all.

The famous sentence is what she does with that finding, and it is more careful than its inspirational-poster afterlife suggests. Mead is not calling for the abolition of difference — the sentence immediately before it says the mere abolition of these distinctions will not produce a society where individual gifts have a place. Her proposal is to keep the richness and change the sorting rule: recognise the whole range of human temperament first, then weave the social fabric around it.
context.detailsSummary: Editions, pagination and the copyright question
detailsBody: The page number in the standard citation, p. 322, belongs to the first edition published by William Morrow in New York in 1935. The edition most readers can buy today is the Harper Perennial centennial reissue of 2001, which runs to 311 pages — so anyone checking p. 322 in a modern paperback will run off the end of the book. That repagination is a plain observation from comparing the two editions, not a claim made by either publisher.

Because the work was first published in 1935, it falls on the copyright side of the pre-1931 line that governs the US public domain in 2026, and it remains in print. Quote it and cite it, but do not treat the text as free.

Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies was published in 1935 by William Morrow and Company, New York; the book compares the Arapesh, Mundugumor and Tchambuli and argues temperamental traits are not inherently sex-linked. NOTE: the article does NOT quote the 'richer culture' passage, and is cited only for publication details and argument.

Margaret Mead was born 16 December 1901 and died 15 November 1978; American cultural anthropologist, curator of ethnology at the American Museum of Natural History (1946-1969), taught at Columbia, Fordham and the University of Rhode Island, author of Coming of Age in Samoa (1928) and Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies (1935), awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom posthumously in 1979.

Quote Investigator found no evidence for 'Never doubt that a small group of thoughtful, committed citizens can change the world' in Mead's works, identifies Donald Keys as the crucial initial propagator, and only tentatively assigns the saying to Mead.

The in-print edition of Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies is the Harper Perennial centennial edition, ISBN 9780060934958, published 2001, 311 pages, with introductions by Helen Fisher and Mary Catherine Bateson; the work was first published in 1935.
